label: Food Intoxication versus Food Infection
rows: A preformed toxin (cells and toxin in the food)
The toxin reaches its target organs
Improper cooking; bacteria multiply in the food, then an intestinal infection

mnemonic.hook: Intoxication: you eat the poison. Infection: you eat the poisoner.
key: infection: live cells that multiply (Salmonella, Listeria)

label: The Seven Foodborne Bacteria
cols: Where it comes from / the food
rows: Human and animal feces; contaminated meats and vegetables
The fecal INDICATOR organism; eosin methylene blue plates confirm it; O157:H7 among the worst
Poultry and aquatic reptiles; eggs, pet food, peanut butter, produce
Young children and the elderly at greatest risk; typhoid the most severe enteric fever
Raw poultry (one drop of its fluid)
Infectious dose under 500 cells; bloody diarrhea; a leading United States bacterial diarrhea
Birds, mammals, soil; soft cheese, deli meats, hot dogs, produce
Grows from 1 to 40 °C; pregnant women and the fetus; slide: number one cause of food-related deaths in the United States
Spores in soil, on plants, in honey
Toxin when spores germinate; flaccid ('relaxed') paralysis, respiratory failure
Very common in summer; onset in 6 hours or less, self-resolving
Salt water: ocean and estuaries; shellfish, oysters, crabs
Water route (including wound infection) or food route

mnemonic.hook: Every Sick Cook Lets Contaminants Breed Vigorously.
mnemonic.breaks: The order is slide 13's list. Two words start with C: Cook (Campylobacter) comes before Contaminants (Clostridium).

rows.note: Slide conflict: standard references say the reverse (the emetic toxin, with rice, is heat-stable; the diarrheal toxin is heat-labile). The quizzes key the slide; see guide 16.17. Slide 28 on the intoxication: onset 6 hours or less, self-resolving vomiting and cramps.

mnemonic.hook: Rice makes you retch; meat sends you running.
mnemonic.breaks: The aid covers the food link only; for heat stability, learn the slide's pairing and the note.

label: Foodborne Viruses
rows: Norwalk-like virus, family Caliciviridae; a common foodborne agent
The hepatitis viruses typically spread by the fecal-oral route
Person to person by feces and vomitus (daycares, nursing homes, cruise ships); contaminated shellfish
Fecal-oral; NOT by kissing, sneezing, saliva or blood
A few viral particles infect; rapid onset and short duration: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, low-grade fever
Most contagious about two weeks BEFORE symptoms

rows.note: Prevention (one list on slide 33, after the hepatitis lines): good handwashing and diaper hygiene, thorough cooking, clean drinking water, and a vaccine in case of suspected exposure.

mnemonic.hook: Noro sails the cruise ship; A and E travel the same road, mouth after bottom.
key: norovirus: crowded places, feces and vomitus, fast in and out
the fecal-oral hepatitis viruses: contagious two weeks before symptoms
